title: Holy and Righteous Simeon the God-Receiver
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, February 3; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: According to the holy Gospel, the elder Simeon was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit rested upon him. God made known to him that the true Messiah would soon come into the world. Ancient historians relate how Simeon received this message. By order of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, the Law of Moses and the books of the prophets were to be translated from Hebrew into Greek. Seventy of the most learned men of the Jewish people were chosen for the work. Simeon was among them, a wise man well acquainted with the divine Scriptures.

While translating the book of Isaiah, Simeon came to the words, “Behold, the Virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” He doubted them, thinking it impossible for a woman without a husband to give birth. He took a knife and was about to scrape the words from the scroll and replace “virgin” with “woman.” At that moment an angel of the Lord appeared, held back his hand, and said, “Believe the words that are written. You yourself will see them fulfilled, for you will not see death before you have seen Christ the Lord, who is to be born of the pure Virgin.”

Believing the words of the angel and the prophet, Simeon eagerly awaited Christ’s coming into the world. He lived a righteous and blameless life, turned away from every evil, and remained constantly in God’s temple. There he prayed that God would have mercy on his world and free its people from the all-deceiving devil.

Forty days after his birth, our Lord Jesus Christ was brought to the temple by the hands of his most pure Mother, as the Law required. Righteous Simeon came there too, led by the Spirit of God. When he saw the eternal Child and the all-pure Virgin who had borne him, he knew that this was the promised Messiah and that she was the Virgin in whom Isaiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled. Seeing her overshadowed by heavenly light and shining with divine rays, he approached in fear and joy, took the divine Child in his arms, and said:

“Now, Master, you let your servant depart in peace according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before all peoples: a light to reveal you to the nations and the glory of your people Israel.”
After this he prophesied Christ’s suffering and crucifixion. He also foretold that a sword of grief and sorrow would pierce the Mother of God’s soul when she saw her Son hanging upon the cross.

Having reached a great old age, Simeon departed to the Lord. It is written of him that he lived for three hundred and sixty years: God had been pleased to prolong the holy elder’s life so that he might live to see the long-awaited year desired by every age, when the ageless Son was born of the Virgin. To him be glory forever. Amen.

title: Venerable Timothy of Symbola
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, February 21; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: Near Mount Olympus was a wilderness place called Symbola, where a monastery stood. Its archimandrite was the virtuous Theoktistos, under whom Venerable Plato the Confessor learned the monastic life. Venerable Timothy was also among Theoktistos’s disciples. From his youth Timothy devoted himself to ascetic labors, striving in fasting and self-restraint and spending whole nights in prayer. Having completely subdued the desires of the flesh, he was free from passions and distinguished by spiritual maturity.

He preserved virginity of soul and body until his death, for from a very early age he had resolved never to look upon a woman’s face. Thus he became a temple of the Holy Spirit and received the gift of healing and power over demons. Many miracles took place through his prayers: he healed every kind of illness and drove unclean spirits from people. For many years he wandered through mountains and wildernesses, living alone in the Lord. In unceasing prayer he shed abundant tears, watering his soul with them as with dew. Living in this way, he reached a great old age and departed to the Lord.

title: Venerable Procopius the Confessor of Decapolis
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, February 27; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: The region of Decapolis, named for its ten cities, lies near the Sea of Galilee. Saint Mark the Evangelist mentions it when he says that Jesus came to the Sea of Galilee through the region of Decapolis. Venerable Procopius the Confessor came from that country. Experienced in monastic struggles and strict fasting, and adorned with purity of soul, he was renowned among ascetics.

Then came the hard days of the iconoclast heresy. Its first instigator, the lawless emperor Leo the Isaurian, falsely called holy icons idols and those who venerated them idol worshippers. He mercilessly killed many innocent Orthodox Christians and condemned the faithful emperors, hierarchs, and Christians who had come before him because they honored the holy icons, and so brought condemnation upon himself. At that time Procopius, a great and unshakable pillar of Orthodoxy and a strong defender of the true faith, bravely stood against the many heretics who in their impiety blasphemed the incarnation of God the Word and dishonored the holy icons. He put them to shame, exposing their foolish reasoning with invincible, God-inspired words, and tore apart their intricate arguments as though they were cobwebs.

He thus brought down the wrath of the godless emperor, who roared like a wild lion seeking prey. At Leo’s command Procopius was seized and cruelly beaten. His tormentors tore his body with iron instruments and cast him into a dark, foul-smelling prison. The saint bore every suffering steadfastly. Venerable Basil, who had earlier struggled alongside Procopius in fasting and virtue, suffered with him. The two endured many torments together for the sake of the holy icons and remained imprisoned until the death of their godless persecutor.

When Leo died, losing not only this passing life but the life to come, Procopius was released with his friend Basil and the other saints. He spent the rest of his life in ascetic labor, guiding many toward virtue and salvation. In venerable old age he departed to Christ God, to see him face to face rather than in an icon, and to receive, as one who had fasted and suffered for Christ and struggled even to bloodshed for his holy image, the fitting reward for his labors.

title: Venerable John Cassian the Roman
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, February 29; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: Venerable Cassian came from Rome and was the son of noble and distinguished parents. From early youth he loved learning and the books of Holy Scripture. Diligent and clear-minded, he first studied philosophy and astronomy, then turned with reverence to Scripture and came to know it so well that he was among the outstanding scholars of his time. He also preserved his virginity and was known for purity of soul, a gracious manner, and other virtues.

Leaving his homeland, he came to Constantinople and Saint John Chrysostom. Having gained further knowledge from him and learned a virtuous way of life, Cassian withdrew to Scetis. In one of the monasteries there he became a monk, giving himself wholly to obedience and every monastic labor, and learning the demanding life of fasting and other ascetic struggles. These labors awakened in him a desire for still higher ones, so he went into the wilderness to live in silence. He spent a long time there, learning to understand temptations and wearing himself out with great toil.

Wishing to learn more from other holy fathers, he left the place where he had kept complete silence and visited the monasteries of Egypt, the Thebaid, Mount Nitria, Asia, Pontus, and Cappadocia. Through these travels he came to know the lives of many great fathers and studied different forms of monastic struggle. Cassian then founded two monasteries in Massilia, one for men and one for women.

He also wrote several books of instruction, filled with wise and useful counsel. Anyone who reads them attentively and diligently can find much benefit for the soul and learn how their holy author lived and discerned. Cassian wrote against Nestorius on the incarnation of God the Word from the most pure Virgin Mother of God. By rightly honoring the Mother of God, he pleased the God born of her. After many years of these labors and struggles, and after giving monks great help through his writings, Saint Cassian departed to the eternal dwellings.

title: Venerable Eumenios, Bishop of Gortyna
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, September 18; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: From his youth, Saint Eumenios pleased God by his virtuous life. He walked the narrow way that leads to the Kingdom of Heaven, mindful of the Lord’s words: ‘Strive to enter through the narrow gate.’ Whoever wishes to pass through that gate must lay down two heavy burdens: concern for possessions and concern for the body. Eumenios gave up his property and distributed it to the poor, remembering how hard it is for a rich person to enter the Kingdom of God.

For how can one who is weighed down by attachment to wealth enter the narrow gate of heaven? The Lord gave good counsel to the young man who asked what he should do to inherit eternal life: ‘If you wish to be perfect,’ He told him, ‘go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.’
One who serves Mammon cannot serve God. Laden with riches, a person can no more pass through the narrow door of heaven than a camel can pass through the eye of a needle.

Anyone passing through a tight place must take off not only a load but even clothing. In the same way, one who desires heaven gives the poor more than the surplus that is troublesome to carry: one gives even what is needed, even the clothing that covers the body, following the Lord’s example. This was how Saint Eumenios lived. He counted everything as refuse, renounced everything, and left everything behind to follow Christ, so that he might gain Christ alone.

Having cast off his property as though it were clothing, he clothed the poor, the naked, and those in need with it. Stripped of earthly attachments, he entered the narrow way of poverty and passed through the gate that leads to heavenly riches. He also laid aside the other burden, concern for the body. Through ascetic struggle, labor, self-restraint, fasting, and vigils he put bodily desires to death and made his body lean, avoiding indulgence and pleasure. As the Apostle says, everyone who strives for mastery exercises self-control in all things.

He abstained from everything that fattens the body, weighs down the mind, and gives rise to passions. He would not allow sleep to his eyes until he had purified soul and body of the passions and become a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. Thus, casting off the heavy burdens of property and bodily passions, he made himself able to travel the narrow way and pass through the gate that leads to eternal life.

Because Eumenios’s virtuous life shone like a lamp and benefited everyone, he was chosen and raised to the episcopal throne of the Church of Gortyna. Like a candle set on a lampstand, he gave light to his flock; like the sun, he illumined the Church of Christ by his deeds and teaching. A light to the world should let deeds come before words, just as a lamp’s glow reaches the eye before the lamp itself is seen.

As bishop, Saint Eumenios therefore taught his spiritual children first by his deeds, by his pure life pleasing to God, giving his flock an example; afterward he taught them by his words. He first became a light himself and then enlightened others. He meditated on the law of the Lord day and night before guiding others in it. Having acquired a clear conscience himself, he helped others to cleanse theirs. True to the meaning of his name, he was deeply merciful, and his life was filled with works of mercy.

He was a father to orphans, wealth to the poor, a giver to those who asked, a comforter of the sorrowful, a healer of the suffering, and a wondrous worker of miracles. Once, by his prayer, he killed a great snake that rushed at him. Yet he worked a still greater wonder when, through prayer, he trampled the serpent of hell, the devil, and drove him away from the flock Christ had entrusted to him. Nor was Gortyna the only place where Eumenios stood against demons: he did so in Rome as well.

When he came to Rome, his signs and wonders astonished many. He drove demons from people, healed the sick, and brought peace to those who were hostile and angry with one another. Later he went to the Thebaid. When rain had failed there, his prayer brought rain down from heaven. In that land he eventually died in peace, passing from this temporary life into life eternal and without end. His holy body was carried back to Gortyna, the place of his ministry, and buried there with honor.

title: The Holy Martyr Zosimas the Hermit
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, September 19; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: One day Dometian, governor of Cilicia, went hunting with his servants. They travelled through many wildernesses, hills, and mountains in pursuit of wild animals. In one place the governor saw a great number of beasts, and among them an old man who walked about and spoke to them as though they were people. The hunters rushed toward them. The animals fled, but the hunters seized the old man and brought him to the governor, supposing that he was a sorcerer working enchantments in the wilderness. Asked who he was and what he was called, the saint answered, “I am a Christian. My name is Zosimas.”

They bound him and brought him into the city for judgment. There the governor questioned him about magic: how had he bewitched the animals so that he could live unharmed among them and talk to them as though they were people? Zosimas answered, “I do not live in the wilderness to practice magic. I am a Christian, and I cannot live in the city among unbelievers. So I went into the wilderness, preferring the company of beasts to that of wicked people, the enemies of my Lord Jesus Christ. I took as my example other Christians, the holy fathers who withdrew from the world to live in the wilderness, and I tried to imitate them as far as I could. God knows those who serve him and cares for them. In his goodness he cared for me also, making the wild animals obedient to me for my comfort. I live with them, rejoicing in the Lord and placing all my hope in him.”

The governor said, “So, wicked old man, you honor the Nazarene? Very well. I shall go to Nazareth and torment you cruelly there. Either you will renounce the Nazarene or lose your life in terrible suffering. And when the Nazarenes see your torments, let them too be afraid.” He sent Zosimas to Nazareth in chains and then went there himself. When he had set a time for the hearing, Dometian ordered Zosimas brought before him and asked, “Tell us about your magic. How did you enchant the beasts?” Zosimas answered by confessing that he was a Christian.

The governor ordered him hung upside down, a heavy stone tied around his neck, and his body torn with iron claws. Then he asked again, “Will you tell us about your magic now?” Zosimas replied, “Christ my God is the one who sent the beasts to comfort me in the wilderness.” The governor said, “If the beasts obey your God, command one to come here. Then we shall all accept your faith.”

Zosimas lifted his hands toward heaven and prayed: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, hear me, your servant. Send a lion here to serve me.” Suddenly a fearsome lion ran into the city, and everyone who saw it fled. The lion came to Zosimas and supported the stone that had been fastened around his neck. The governor begged him, “Zosimas, calm the beast, and we shall untie you.” Zosimas commanded the lion to be gentle. The governor ordered the saint released and wanted to send him to the emperor, but Zosimas gave up his spirit to God. The Christians buried his body with honor, glorifying the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is glorified forever. Amen.

title: The Holy Apostle Ananias of the Seventy
source: St. Dimitry of Rostov, Lives of the Saints, October 1; complete English translation of the featured life from the public-domain Russian edition
paragraphs: The holy Apostle Ananias, one of the Seventy, was bishop in the city of Damascus. He is known for baptizing the Apostle Paul. Once the Lord appeared to him in a vision and said, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul; he is praying there.”

Ananias hesitated, knowing how much harm Saul had done to the Christians in Jerusalem and that he had come to Damascus intending to bind all who confessed the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. But the Lord urged Ananias on: “Go, for Saul is my chosen vessel to proclaim my name before nations and kings and the children of Israel, and I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.”

Obeying the divine command, Ananias went to Saul, laid his hands on him, and said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Saul immediately regained his sight, and Ananias baptized him.

Later, when the Jews plotted to kill Paul because the former persecutor had become a preacher of Christ’s name, Ananias and the other disciples lowered him in a basket over the city wall. Ananias himself went into the Jewish synagogues and boldly preached the Lord’s name. He proclaimed the Christian faith not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles.

From Damascus he went to Eleutheropolis. There he showed people the way of salvation, healed the sick, and brought many to faith in Christ. In those days the governor of Eleutheropolis was Lucian, who worshipped the creature rather than the Creator. The devil stirred him against the Christians, and he sent this order throughout his territory: “Anyone found honoring Christ and worshipping the Crucified One is to be tortured to death. Whoever renounces Christ and sacrifices to the immortal gods shall receive gifts and honors from us.”

After this wicked and cunning order was issued, holy Ananias continued to enlighten the people of that region by preaching the Gospel and to cure every kind of sickness among them. The Lord was with him and worked many miracles through him. Idol worshippers seized Ananias and brought him before Lucian, who tried by many means to force him to sacrifice to the idols. Ananias would not obey.

He answered, “I will not worship false gods. I worship the one true Lord, my God Jesus Christ. I have seen him with my own eyes and spoken with him face to face, not only while he lived on earth as a man but also after his ascension into heaven. When I was in Damascus, he himself appeared to me and sent me to heal Saul, whom by his wondrous wisdom and power he had brought to knowledge of the truth. He freed us all from the power of the devil and led us to his Father. It is he whom I worship, not the demons who seek to destroy all humankind.”

The governor then threatened Ananias with torments unless he did as he was commanded. But Ananias, like an unshakable pillar, stood firm in his confession of Christ. Raising his hands toward heaven, he prayed: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the blessed Father, hear my prayer and grant me a share with the blessed apostles in the life to come. As you saved Saul by your light, so save me from the hand of this godless man who opposes the truth. Do not let his will prevail over me or let him catch me in his deceitful snares. Do not deprive me of the kingdom of heaven prepared for all who love the way of your truth, which you have shown, and keep your commandments.”

Unable to bear Ananias’s words any longer, the governor ordered him laid on the ground and beaten. While the servants beat the saint without mercy, a herald cried out, “Obey the governor. Do not resist his command. Sacrifice to the gods whom all the world worships.”

When they stopped beating him, the governor said, “At least take pity on yourself now. Listen to me and renounce the Crucified One, or I will subject you to still worse torments.” Ananias replied, “What I told you at the beginning I say again now: I will not deny my God, nor will I bow before the lifeless stone and wood you honor as gods.”

Seeing that the saint would not yield, the governor ordered his body torn with iron claws and his wounds burned with candles. As Ananias endured the torture, he lifted his eyes toward heaven and prayed earnestly. Afterward his tormentor said, “How long will you remain stubborn? Will you not take pity on yourself and worship the great gods? Is it really preferable to suffer these useless torments for some Christ whom the Jews crucified, rather than be safe and well? I swear I will not let you leave my hands alive if you persist.”

The saint answered, “Do what you wish, enemy of God and friend of the devil. You have heard me many times: I will not worship your gods. I worship the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Creator of heaven and earth and all that is in them. I have believed in him, and he has given me strength to stand firmly before you all day and bear these torments with courage. Why trouble yourself any longer? You know I will not obey your will. Do quickly what you have resolved to do.”

Burning with anger, the tormentor ordered the people to take Ananias outside the city and stone him. The lawless servants led him to the place of execution and stoned him like another Stephen. He cried aloud, “Lord Jesus Christ, into your hands I entrust my spirit.”

Thus, after all his sufferings, he died and passed into the heavenly dwellings. When the people saw that he was dead, they left him unburied and went away. Some Christians from Damascus happened to pass by. They took the holy body of Christ’s apostle, carried it with honor to Damascus, and buried him in his own city.
